Filament

FIL-uh-munt -- Latin filum, 'thread': a filament is a fine thread of something. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Filament is a slender, threadlike object or fiber.

Inside the old light bulb, a tiny tungsten filament glowed white-hot.

Worked Example

Under a microscope, a single strand of spider silk looks like a shining wire thinner than a human hair, yet strong enough to hold a struggling insect.

That fine, threadlike strand is exactly what a filament is. Unlike 'cable,' which bundles many strands into something thick, a filament is a single delicate thread.

How Strong Is It? — strand → fiber → filament

strand vs. filament

strand vs. filament: Strand is a close, everyday cousin of filament -- a strand can be any single thin length, while filament usually emphasizes something especially fine, delicate, or technical.

fiber vs. filament

fiber vs. filament: Fiber is a broader material word than filament: fibers are the threadlike stuff things are made of, while a filament is one specific slender thread, like the glowing wire inside a bulb.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — fil-

root — fil-: thread (Latin (filum))

suffix — -ment

suffix — -ment: noun-forming: the result or thing produced (Latin (-mentum))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin filum meant 'thread,' and filamentum named something spun out into a thread -- a filament is literally 'a threaded thing,' the same root behind filigree, jewelry made of fine twisted threads of metal.

Use the root in a new word: filigree
